CHAPTER XXII

The effect was so sudden and magical, that the shooter himself was
stupefied for an instant. Then he hailed his companions to join him in
effecting the capture, and himself set off up the hill; but, ere he had
got half way, up rose the figure of Martin Wittenhaagen with a bent bow
in his hand. Eric Wouverman no sooner saw him in this attitude, than he
darted behind a tree, and made himself as small as possible. Martin's
skill with that weapon was well known, and the slain dog was a keen
reminder of it.

Wouverman peered round the bark cautiously: there was the arrow's point
still aimed at him. He saw it shine. He dared not move from his shelter.

When he had been at peep-ho some minutes, his companions came up in
great force.

Then, with a scornful laugh, Martin vanished, and presently was heard to
ride off on the mule.

All the men ran up together. The high ground commanded a view of a
narrow but almost interminable glade.

They saw Gerard and Margaret running along at a prodigious distance;
they looked like gnats; and Martin galloping after them ventre a terre.

The hunters were outwitted as well as outrun. A few words will explain
Martin's conduct. We arrive at causes by noting coincidences; yet, now
and then, coincidences are deceitful. As we have all seen a hare tumble
over a briar just as the gun went off, and so raise expectations, then
dash them to earth by scudding away untouched, so the burgomaster's mule
put her foot in a rabbit-hole at or about the time the crossbow bolt
whizzed innocuous over her head: she fell and threw both her riders.
Gerard caught Margaret, but was carried down by her weight and impetus;
and, behold, the soil was strewed with dramatis personae.

The docile mule was up again directly, and stood trembling. Martin was
next, and looking round saw there was but one in pursuit; on this he
made the young lovers fly on foot, while he checked the enemy as I have
recorded.

He now galloped after his companions, and when after a long race he
caught them, he instantly put Gerard and Margaret on the mule, and ran
by their side till his breath failed, then took his turn to ride, and so
in rotation. Thus the runner was always fresh, and long ere they relaxed
their speed all sound and trace of them was hopelessly lost to Dierich
and his men. These latter went crestfallen back to look after their
chief and their winged bloodhound.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER TWO.
[Reference Rewrite]: To comprehend the architecture of my early exile, one must first understand the absolute poverty of my universe at the age of seven. I existed within a microscopic empire of two, subjugated by a man I was conditioned to call "Master." He was a square-built, brutal artifact of a world I did not know, roughly sixty years of age, though time on the island seemed measured only by the decay of his humanity. His dark hair fell in matted, feral clusters, and a vast beard obscured his face, rendering him less a man than a beast draped in the ruin of whatever civilization had cast him out. He possessed a terrifying latent power, yet he spent his days in a state of stagnant lethargy, only stirring to exert his dominance over my labor—collecting sea-birds or hauling faggots of wood down the ravine.

Our lives were bound by the daily ritual of bathing in a salt-water pool, barricaded from the shark-infested ocean by a ridge of jagged stone. Beyond this, my existence was an enforced void. I was permitted no education, no heritage, and almost no language. The Master utilized silence as a tool of oppression, rationing his words to commands and curses, ensuring my mind remained as barren as the rocky crags that caged us. I became a taciturn creature, my intellect starved, left to gaze into the abyssal depths of the ocean or trace the cold geometries of the stars. I was kept as a beast of the field—valuable only for the calories my labor saved him, and perhaps to serve as a mirror for his own desperate need for mastery.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER THREE.

I left him, and commenced a careful descent of the precipices by which we were surrounded, but, before I had gone fifty paces, another flash of lightning was followed up by a loud shriek, which arrested my steps. Where the noise came from I could not tell, but I heard my companion calling to me to come back. I obeyed him, and found him standing where I had left him.

"You called me, master?"

"Yes, I did; take my hand and lead me to the cabin."

I obeyed him, wondering why he asked me so to do. He gained his bed-place, and threw himself down on it.

"Bring the kid full of water," said he--"quick!"

I brought it, and he bathed his head and face. After a time, he threw himself back upon the bed-place, and groaned heavily.

"O God! It's all over with me," said he at last. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What's the matter, master?" said I.
[Reference Rewrite]: I left him in the dark, initiating a careful descent down the rain-slicked precipices that formed the carceral walls of our world. Before I had traversed fifty paces, a sudden rupture of lightning tore the sky, pursued instantly by a shriek so guttural it arrested my breath. It was a sound stripped of all former sovereignty. I could not trace its origin through the howling wind, but then I heard the voice—his voice, diminished and frantic—commanding my return.

I obeyed, stepping back over the jagged stone, and found him frozen exactly where I had left him.

"You called me, master?" I asked, testing the word on my tongue.

"Yes, I did. Take my hand. Lead me to the cabin."

I guided him, marveling at the sudden frailty in his grip. The hand that had so often struck me down now clung to my shoulder with the desperate dependency of a drowning man. He found his bedding and collapsed onto it, a ruined monument of flesh.

"Bring the kid full of water," he gasped. "Quick!"

I brought the vessel. He plunged his face into it, bathing his head as if trying to wash away the fire of the heavens. Presently, he fell back against the damp wood, a heavy groan escaping his chest. "O God! It is all over with me," he whispered into the gloom. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What is the matter, master?" I asked.

He offered no answer, sinking instead into a rhythmic liturgy of curses and moans. When he finally fell still, I slipped out again into the dying tempest.

The discharge was instantaneous, a sudden, magical rupture in the air that left the shooter momentarily stupefied. Only then did he hail his companions to join him in the pursuit, launching himself up the hill. But scarcely had he covered half the ascent when the silhouette of Martin Wittenhaagen emerged, a bent bow drawn taut in his hand. Upon seeing Martin poised thus, Eric Wouverman instinctively darted behind the nearest tree, shrinking his form until he was nothing more than a shadow against the bark. Martin's mastery with the weapon was legendary, and the lifeless dog lying nearby served as a grim testament to his lethal precision.

Wouverman peered cautiously around the rough hide of the tree; there, fixed in the wood, was the arrowhead, gleaming with a malevolent intent. It was aimed directly at him. Terrified, he dared not shift his position. Minutes passed in tense silence as he held his breath, waiting for the inevitable strike. Finally, his companions arrived in overwhelming numbers. With a derisive laugh, Martin vanished from sight, and shortly thereafter, the sound of his mule's hooves echoed as he rode away. The remaining hunters surged forward, only to find themselves outwitted and outrun.

From the commanding height, the glade stretched out—a narrow corridor seemingly without end. Far below, they spotted Gerard and Margaret sprinting across the grass, appearing no larger than gnats. Behind them thundered Martin, driving the mule *ventre à terre*, his legs pumping furiously. The hunters had been bested not merely by speed, but by cunning.

To understand Martin's audacious strategy, one must look beyond mere coincidence, for while chance often mimics design, it rarely orchestrates such precise chaos. Just as a startled hare might tumble over a briar precisely when a shot rings out, raising false hopes before vanishing unharmed, so too did fate intervene here. At the very moment the crossbow bolt whistled harmlessly overhead, the burgomaster's mule stepped squarely into a hidden rabbit-hole. She stumbled, collapsing under the combined weight of her riders. Gerard caught Margaret in his arms, but her momentum dragged him down with her, scattering the principal actors across the soil like fallen leaves.

The docile mule rose immediately, trembling violently, while Martin scrambled up beside her. Seeing that only one pursuer remained, he executed a brilliant tactical pivot: he urged the terrified mule onward, forcing the young lovers to flee on foot, while he personally engaged the lone hunter. Once he had secured his companions, he mounted them both, running alongside the mule until his lungs burned, then swapping places with Gerard. In this relentless rotation, the runners never fatigued. Long before the exhausted hunters could recover, every trace of the fugitives was erased from the landscape. Defeated and crestfallen, Dierich and his men turned back, leaving behind their leader and his winged bloodhound to mourn their failure.
